# Āneñjasappāya Sutta (MN 106 (PTS MN ii 261))

**ID:** MN 106 (PTS MN ii 261)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Āneñjasappāya Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Conducive to the Imperturbable
**PTS:** MN ii 261
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn106
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Āneñjasappāya Sutta* ("Conducive to the Imperturbable", MN 106 / PTS MN ii 261) is a discourse in the Majjhimanikāya outlining progressive paths toward meditative absorption, the formless attainments, and final liberation [SuttaCentral; Rogell 2003]. Opening with the admonition that sensual pleasures are impermanent, hollow, and deceptive (*māyākatam*) [Westerhoff 2018], the Buddha details how practitioners can transcend the disturbances of sensuality and material forms by cultivating the "imperturbable" (*āneñja*), a state associated with the fourth *jhāna* and higher meditative states [Pande 1974; Rogell 2003; Polak 2011]. The discourse presents specific reflective approaches leading to the dimension of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), including the contemplation that the cessation of perceptions is peaceful, the insight into selflessness, and the reflection that one does not belong to anything [Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation; Thanissaro 2013]. A central doctrinal emphasis of the sutta is that subtle equanimity (*upekkhā*) reached at these refined levels must not become an object of attachment; clinging must be relinquished through reflections such as "what exists, what has become, that I abandon" (*yad atthi, yaṁ bhūtaṁ taṁ pajahāmi*) so that consciousness becomes unestablished (*apatiṭṭhita*) and achieves complete liberation [Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation; Thanissaro 2013]. Grzegorz Polak notes that the sutta contains a distinctive meditative schema wherein the higher formless dimensions are preceded directly by *āneñja* rather than the standard fourfold formless sequence [Polak 2011].

A full parallel to the sutta is found in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 75), and the text is cited in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 19.2) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies cross-language text reuse with Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094), the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and Chinese Āgama texts (*Madhyama-āgama* T 26 and *Saṁyukta-āgama* T 99) [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records 1,021 matching text segments across 67 texts, sharing substantial formulaic material with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), *Sattakanipāta* (AN 7), *Kosambiya Sutta* (MN 48), and *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), as well as exegesis in the *Pañcapakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā* and *Majjhimanikāye Uparipaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
